extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical mechanics (undergraduate/graduate level); physics/engineering learners
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the principle of virtual velocities/displacements and related equilibrium criteria in statics, with definitions, historical attributions, sign conventions, limiting conditions, and worked examples (pulleys, levers, wheel-and-axle, three-knot problem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelogram of forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Once we have been led to the principle of the parallelogram of forces ... the principle is just as much an observation as any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent two forces by lines and construct the parallelogram on them; the resultant is the diagonal; supply a force equal and opposite to the resultant and the three forces will be in equilibrium at the angles given by the construction. Experimental demonstrations (Cauchy's apparatus: three threads over grooved wheels on a divided circle) illustrate that three equal forces acting at angles of 120° are in equilibrium. Use to reduce difficult observations to simpler, more easily obtained ones when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of virtual velocities (general enunciation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For equilibrium the sum of the products of the forces into their virtual velocities (projections of infinitesimal compatible displacements on the directions of the forces) must vanish: Σ P p = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define virtual velocities (virtual displacements) as infinitely small displacements compatible with the connections/constraints; take projections of those displacements on the force directions (positive if in same direction as the force, negative otherwise). Apply Σ P p = 0 to obtain equilibrium conditions for arbitrary systems of forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of virtual displacements
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtual displacements are displacements consistent with the character of the connections of a system and with one another (infinitely small, compatible movements permitted by constraints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: points connected by a rectangularly bent lever have arc displacements with fixed ratio; points connected by a thread slipping through rings move on spherical surfaces with radii satisfying r1 + r2 + CD = L. Use infinitesimal displacements to avoid carrying system into a different adjacent configuration; judge equilibrium only by vanishingly small displacements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign convention for virtual moments/projections
rubrics_metrics.description: Projections of virtual displacements on the directions of the forces are considered positive when they fall in the direction of the force and negative when opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The products P·p are called virtual moments and may have contrary signs depending on direction. Maintain consistent sign convention when summing virtual moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galileo's work criterion (sum of works = 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equilibrium criterion: the sum of the products of weights and their (simultaneously possible) vertical displacements is zero: P h + P' h' + P'' h'' + ... = 0. This sum is identified with 'work'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by inclined plane and pulleys: equilibrium determined by both weights and their possible approach to/retreat from earth's centre. Use work as decisive factor in many equilibrium problems; experimental knowledge precedes philosophical choice of criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torricelli / centre-of-gravity formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Equilibrium exists when, under an admissible displacement, the centre of gravity of the attached weights cannot descend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent to Galileo's formulation; use centre-of-gravity reasoning to test whether possible displacements would allow the centre of gravity to descend. If centre of gravity cannot descend for any virtual displacement, system is in equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statical moments as an alternative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier investigators used statical moments (weights × distances from axis of rotation) as decisive factors for equilibrium (e.g., for wheel and axle equilibrium PR = Qr).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statical moments and work are alternative measures; choice of criterion (moments or work) may be guided by convenience and the problem's symmetry. Both are valid where applicable and equivalent in many simple cases (e.g., levers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent-point condition: vanishing virtual moment
rubrics_metrics.description: If all material points on which forces act are independent of each other, each point can be in equilibrium only if its virtual moment vanishes separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When displacements are independent, the condition ΣPp = 0 reduces to each Pp = 0; treat dependent and independent points accordingly when decomposing the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: General condition with irreversible displacements (inequality form)
rubrics_metrics.description: When displacements are not all reversible (some virtual displacements cannot be reversed), the general condition of equilibrium is that the sum of the virtual moments is equal to or less than zero (Σ P p ≤ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inequality arises because some admissible displacements could allow the centre of gravity to rise while the reverse descent is impossible; retain the more general '≤ 0' condition in presence of constraints like inextensible strings, contact without penetration, or unilateral constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of infinitesimals (why infinitesimal virtual displacements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinitely small displacements are used instead of finite motions because a system might be carried into an entirely different configuration by a finite displacement for which equilibrium would not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict virtual displacements to vanishingly small amounts so they probe the immediate tendency of the system without crossing into adjacent configurations that change constraints or connectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement of arbitrary forces by equivalent weight-string systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Any force can be replaced by the pull of a heavy body on a string; replace forces by strings passing over pulleys and attach appropriate weights so the condition Σ P p = 0 asserts that the centre of gravity of the system of weights cannot descend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device justifies applying the principle discovered for heavy bodies to any forces; it is used to interpret virtual work conditions in terms of potential descent/ascent of an equivalent weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lagrange reduction via integer-turn pulley representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace forces by a single common measure Q/2 and represent each force P, P', ... by an integral multiple of this measure via ideal pulleys (n, n', ... turns). Then the equilibrium condition (projections positive) can be expressed in terms of the number of turns and projections: 2 n p + 2 n' p' + ... < 0, equivalently Σ n_i·(projection)_i ≤ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constructive reduction shows how to combine forces into a single representative weight and derive the virtual work condition; useful as an existence/constructive proof of the virtual work principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application economy: reduce complex machines to two-point displacement test
rubrics_metrics.description: If only two points are exposed as points of application (with simultaneous displacements h and h'), equilibrium is P h = P' h' regardless of internal construction of the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principle saves detailed analysis of internal components: knowing displacements at application points suffices to state the equilibrium condition—useful when machine is hidden or complicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-equal-forces junction geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: For three equal forces meeting at a common knot and supporting equal weights, equilibrium requires each pair of strings to make 120° with each other (angles at knot sum to 360° with equal separation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by displacing knot O in arbitrary planar directions and applying Σ virtual moments = 0, leading to cos relations that yield angles of 120°. Use geometric constructions (equilateral triangles and circumcircles) to locate knot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worked-example method: derive equilibrium equations from Σ P p = 0
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the virtual moments sum zero to derive specific equilibrium relations for particular machines (e.g., wheel and axle, differential pulley, suspended wheel-and-axle with two cords, double cylinder with friction, Roberval balance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up virtual displacements consistent with constraints, compute projections on force directions, form Σ P p and set = 0 (or ≤ 0 for irreversible cases), then solve for unknown forces or geometrical relations. Be careful with sign, dependence of displacements, and limiting cases (e.g., R = r leading to indeterminacy).
